title: Apocock
summary: A Shinnecock–Unkechaug boundary creek where a 1665 agreement protected both nations’ access to marsh plants on either bank.
map_geometry_source: Approximate modern point for Beaverdam Creek, historically associated with Apocock/Apaucuck; not an exact historic coordinate.
why_this_matters: Apocock connects the Beaverdam Creek area to wetland plants, meadowland, and the practical materials of Native coastal life. Its interpretation as flaggy land or a covering-place points to reeds and other plants used for mats, shelters, and everyday work, while related records also place the creek within a broader Native territorial landscape. Wetlands were knowledgeable homelands shaped by language, ecology, and community use, not empty margins.
introduction_content: At Apocock, a boundary did not end the right to use a wetland. A 1665 agreement identified the middle of this creek as a boundary between Shinnecock and Unkechaug lands while allowing people of both nations to cut marsh plants on either bank. Tooker, pp. 14–15
history_content: The agreement, recorded before Governor Richard Nicolls, reserved shared access to the “flags” used for practical purposes. Tooker connected Apocock with plants used for mats and coverings, placing everyday knowledge of wetlands alongside political boundary-making. The record describes neighboring Native nations negotiating use of a shared resource; it does not describe an empty shore awaiting settlement. Tooker, pp. 14–15
translation_content:
Apocock is treated as a variation of Appaquogue and is interpreted as flaggy land or wigwam-covering place. Recorded forms include Apaucuck, Apocuck, Appocock, Apockac, and Apocock. The shared interpretation does not make this the same site as East Hampton Appaquogue. Pawcuck is also recorded as a Westhampton neck form cross-referenced to Apocuck.

Why Place Names Matter

“Indigenous place names have existed for thousands of years, reflecting deep connections to land, water, and community.”

— BC Geographical Names Office, BC Geographical Names Office (2026), Indigenous Tag section

Apocock connects the Beaverdam Creek area to wetland plants, meadowland, and the practical materials of Native coastal life. Its interpretation as flaggy land or a covering-place points to reeds and other plants used for mats, shelters, and everyday work, while related records also place the creek within a broader Native territorial landscape. Wetlands were knowledgeable homelands shaped by language, ecology, and community use, not empty margins.
whereintheworld_content: The pin marks Beaverdam Creek in present-day Westhampton, the modern waterway identified with Apocock/Apaucock. The historical name also covered adjoining upland and meadow east of the creek. A point in the waterway cannot define that entire tract, and no exact land polygon is asserted here. This is distinct from Appaquogue in East Hampton. Tooker, pp. 14–15
